guides.title: Troubleshoot Windows Services
guides.symptom: A Windows service keeps crashing, won't start, or is causing errors
guides.description: Learn to manage Windows services — diagnose service failures, fix dependencies, and restart or reconfigure services using services.msc and command-line tools.
causes: Service depends on another service that isn't running
Service executable file is corrupted or missing
Wrong logon account configured for the service
Port conflict with another application
Corrupted system files affecting the service
guides.whyItWorks: Windows services are background programs that run without a user interface — they handle networking, printing, updates, and much more. Each service can depend on other services, run under specific user accounts, and use specific ports. When a service fails, the issue is usually a broken dependency chain, a corrupted executable, or wrong permissions. Checking dependencies ensures the foundation is solid, restarting the service clears temporary glitches, and Event Viewer reveals the specific error message that tells you exactly what went wrong.

steps.instruction: Open Services console and identify the service
steps.detail: Press Windows+R, type 'services.msc' and press Enter. Find the service in question — they're listed alphabetically. Note its Status (Running, Stopped, empty) and Startup Type (Automatic, Manual, Disabled). Double-click the service to see its properties.

In the service Properties window, click the 'Dependencies' tab. This shows two lists: services this service depends on (must be running first) and services that depend on this service. Go back to the services list and check if all dependency services are running. Start any stopped dependencies first.

In the service Properties > Log On tab, check which account runs the service. Most system services use 'Local System', 'Local Service', or 'Network Service'. If it was changed to a specific user account, that account may have had its password changed or lost permissions. Try setting it back to 'Local System account' if appropriate.

Click 'Start' in the service Properties, or right-click the service > Start. If it fails, note the exact error message and error code. Common errors:
• Error 1053: Service did not respond in time — may be corrupted
• Error 1067: Process terminated unexpectedly — check Event Viewer
• Error 1069: Logon failure — check the Log On account
• Error 5: Access denied — run services.msc as Administrator

steps.instruction: Check Event Viewer for detailed error information
steps.detail: Press Windows+R, type 'eventvwr.msc'. Navigate to Windows Logs > System (for system services) or Application (for app services). Look for Error or Warning events around the time the service failed. The event details will show the specific reason for the failure, including error codes and stack traces that can help identify the root cause.

steps.instruction: Use command-line tools for advanced management
steps.detail:
Open Command Prompt as Administrator. Useful commands:

sc query [servicename] — Check service status
sc config [servicename] start= auto — Set startup type to automatic
sc stop [servicename] — Stop a service
sc start [servicename] — Start a service
sc failure [servicename] reset= 86400 actions= restart/60000 — Auto-restart on failure

Replace [servicename] with the actual service name (not display name). Find the service name in its Properties > General tab.

steps.instruction: Run SFC and DISM to repair corrupted service files
steps.detail:
Open Command Prompt as Administrator:

sfc /scannow
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth

These commands repair corrupted Windows system files, which may include service executables and DLLs. Restart after completion and try starting the service again.

guides.title: Safe Registry Editing for Common Fixes
guides.symptom: I need to fix a setting that isn't available in the normal Settings app
guides.description: Learn how to safely navigate, back up, and edit the Windows Registry for fixes that go beyond the standard Settings interface.
causes: Settings app doesn't expose all Windows configuration options
A previous program or malware changed registry values
Need to apply a fix recommended by Microsoft support
Want to disable or enable hidden Windows features
guides.whyItWorks: The Windows Registry is a hierarchical database that stores all of Windows' configuration settings — from desktop wallpaper to deep system behavior. The Settings app only exposes a fraction of these settings. When you need to change something Settings can't reach, the Registry Editor (regedit) gives you direct access. Always backing up before editing ensures you can undo any mistakes. The registry is organized into 'hives' (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE for system-wide, HKEY_CURRENT_USER for your account), 'keys' (folders), and 'values' (individual settings).

steps.instruction: Create a System Restore point first
steps.detail: Before ANY registry editing, create a restore point. Search 'Create a restore point' in Start menu > click 'Create' > name it 'Before Registry Edit' > click Create. This lets you completely undo any changes by restoring from this point if something goes wrong.
steps.warning: CRITICAL: Always create a restore point before editing the registry. Incorrect registry changes can make Windows unbootable.

steps.instruction: Open Registry Editor and back up
steps.detail: Press Windows+R, type 'regedit' and press Enter. Click 'Yes' on the UAC prompt. Before making changes, export a backup: click File > Export > set 'Export range' to 'All' > save the .reg file to your Desktop. If anything goes wrong, you can double-click this file to restore the backup.
steps.warning: The Registry Editor has no undo button. Incorrect edits can cause programs to stop working or prevent Windows from starting. Always back up first.

steps.detail:
The registry has five root keys:

• HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU) — Settings for your user account
• HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM) — System-wide settings for all users
• HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT — File type associations
• HKEY_USERS — Settings for all user profiles
• HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG — Hardware profile settings

Navigate by expanding folders in the left pane. Values appear in the right pane. You can also press Ctrl+F to search or paste a full path into the address bar at the top.

Here are frequently needed registry edits:

1. DISABLE Bing search in Start menu: HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer — create DWORD 'DisableSearchBoxSuggestions' set to 1

2. SHOW file extensions always: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced — set 'HideFileExt' to 0

3. ADD 'Open Command Prompt here' to right-click: HKCU\Software\Classes\Directory\Background\shell\cmd — create key and set default value

4. DISABLE lock screen (Pro only alternative): HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Personalization — create DWORD 'NoLockScreen' set to 1

To edit: navigate to the path, right-click in the right pane > New > DWORD (32-bit) Value, name it, then double-click to set the value.

Navigate to the key containing the value you want to change. In the right pane, double-click the value name. A dialog appears showing the current data. Modify the value:

• DWORD values: Enter a number (0 often means disabled, 1 means enabled)
• String values: Enter text
• Binary values: Edit the hex data (advanced)

Click OK to save. Some changes take effect immediately, others require signing out or restarting.

If something goes wrong after editing the registry:

1. If Windows still works: Double-click the .reg backup file you exported to restore those values, or use System Restore to go back to your restore point.

2. If Windows won't start: Boot to Advanced Startup Options (hold Shift while clicking Restart, or let it fail to boot 3 times) > Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore > select your restore point.

guides.title: Configure Group Policy Settings
guides.symptom: I need to control Windows behavior that the Settings app doesn't offer
guides.description: Use Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc) to manage advanced Windows settings like update behavior, lock screen, and security policies.
causes: Need to configure automatic update behavior
Want to disable features like Cortana or lock screen
Need to enforce security settings
Settings app doesn't provide the level of control needed
guides.whyItWorks: Group Policy is Windows' enterprise-grade configuration tool. It allows IT administrators (and power users) to control nearly every aspect of Windows behavior through a structured interface. Policies override normal settings and are harder for programs or updates to change. When you modify a policy, Windows writes the corresponding registry values and enforces them. Running 'gpupdate /force' immediately applies changes without waiting for the regular refresh cycle.

steps.instruction: Check if your Windows edition supports Group Policy
steps.detail: Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc) is only available on Windows 10/11 Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions. Home edition does NOT include it. To check your edition: Settings > System > About > look for 'Edition'. If you have Home edition, you'll need to use the Registry Editor instead for similar changes.
steps.warning: Group Policy Editor is NOT available on Windows Home editions. These steps only work on Pro, Enterprise, or Education editions.

steps.detail:
Press Windows+R, type 'gpedit.msc' and press Enter. The editor opens with two main sections:

• Computer Configuration — Settings that apply to the entire computer regardless of who logs in
• User Configuration — Settings that apply only to user accounts

Each section has 'Software Settings', 'Windows Settings', and 'Administrative Templates'. Most useful policies are under Administrative Templates.

Navigate to these paths for frequently needed settings:

1. CONTROL Windows Update restart behavior:
Computer Config > Admin Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > 'No auto-restart with logged on users' — set to Enabled

2. DISABLE Cortana:
Computer Config > Admin Templates > Windows Components > Search > 'Allow Cortana' — set to Disabled

3. DISABLE telemetry/diagnostic data:
Computer Config > Admin Templates > Windows Components > Data Collection > 'Allow Diagnostic Data' — set to Enabled, select 'Diagnostic data off'

4. PREVENT app installations:
Computer Config > Admin Templates > Windows Components > Windows Installer > 'Prohibit User Installs' — set to Enabled

Double-click any policy to see its description, options, and help text.

After changing policies, open Command Prompt as Administrator and run:

gpupdate /force

This immediately applies all policy changes. Without this, policies refresh automatically every 90 minutes. You may need to restart your computer for some policies to take full effect.

Open Command Prompt as Administrator and run:

gpresult /r

This shows all currently applied group policies for both the computer and your user account. For a detailed HTML report:

gpresult /h C:\GPReport.html

Open the HTML file in your browser for a comprehensive view of all applied policies.

guides.title: Fix Driver Issues and Blue Screen Crashes
guides.symptom: I get blue screens (BSOD) or hardware stopped working after an update
guides.description: Diagnose and fix driver-related crashes including Blue Screen of Death (BSOD), from safe mode recovery to driver rollback and clean reinstallation.
causes: Windows Update installed an incompatible driver
Manually installed wrong or corrupted driver
Driver conflict between two hardware devices
Hardware failure that the driver can't handle
Corrupted driver files on disk
guides.whyItWorks: Drivers are the software that lets Windows communicate with hardware (graphics cards, network adapters, USB devices, etc.). When a driver has a bug, is incompatible, or is corrupted, it can cause a system crash (Blue Screen of Death) because drivers run with high system privileges. Rolling back to a previous working driver undoes the bad update. Safe Mode loads only essential drivers, letting you fix the problem without the faulty driver interfering. The BSOD stop code tells you exactly which driver or component crashed.

steps.instruction: Note the Blue Screen stop code
steps.detail:
When you get a Blue Screen, note the stop code shown at the bottom (e.g., IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION, VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE). Also note any file name mentioned (e.g., nvlddmkm.sys = NVIDIA driver, igdkmd64.sys = Intel graphics). This tells you which driver is likely responsible.

Common stop codes:
• VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE — Graphics driver crash
• IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL — Usually a network or USB driver
• SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION — Can be any driver
• KMODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED — Often a specific driver mentioned

If Windows keeps crashing: let it fail to boot 3 times and it will enter Automatic Repair > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart > press 4 or F4 for Safe Mode (or 5/F5 for Safe Mode with Networking).

If Windows still works: Hold Shift while clicking Start > Power > Restart. Then Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart > press 4.

Safe Mode loads minimal drivers so you can fix the problematic one.

In Safe Mode (or normal mode if stable), open Device Manager (Windows+X > Device Manager). Find the device with the problematic driver (look for devices with yellow triangle warnings). Right-click > Properties > Driver tab > click 'Roll Back Driver'. If available, this reverts to the previously installed driver. If the button is grayed out, the previous driver wasn't saved.

In Device Manager, right-click the device > 'Uninstall device'. CHECK the box 'Delete the driver software for this device' (important!). Click Uninstall. Restart your computer. Windows will install a default driver.

Then download the latest stable driver from the manufacturer's website (NOT from third-party driver update tools):
• NVIDIA: nvidia.com/drivers
• AMD: amd.com/en/support
• Intel: intel.com/download
• Others: check the device manufacturer's support page
steps.warning: Uninstalling a graphics driver will temporarily reduce your screen resolution. This is normal and will be fixed once the new driver is installed.

steps.instruction: Block Windows from auto-updating the driver
steps.detail:
If Windows keeps reinstalling a problematic driver via Windows Update, you can block it. Open Command Prompt as Administrator and run the driver blocking tool:

1. Download 'Show or Hide Updates' troubleshooter from Microsoft (search 'wushowhide.diagcab')
2. Run it and select 'Hide updates'
3. Select the driver update you want to block
4. Click Next to hide it from Windows Update

Alternatively via Group Policy (Pro editions): Computer Configuration > Admin Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > 'Do not include drivers with Windows Updates' — Enabled.

steps.instruction: Use Driver Verifier to find the culprit (advanced)
steps.detail:
If you can't identify which driver is crashing, open Command Prompt as Admin and run:

verifier /standard /all

Restart your computer. Driver Verifier applies extra stress-testing to all drivers. If a driver is faulty, it will crash immediately with the driver name in the BSOD. After identifying the driver, disable Verifier with:

verifier /reset

And restart again.
steps.warning: Driver Verifier WILL cause a blue screen if any driver has issues. Only use this for diagnosis. Make sure you know how to boot into Safe Mode to disable it.

guides.title: Fix Device Manager Errors and Unknown Devices
guides.symptom: Device Manager shows errors (yellow triangles) or unknown devices
guides.description: Resolve Device Manager error codes, identify unknown devices, and install the correct drivers.
causes: Driver not installed for a device (Code 28)
Device failed to start due to driver issues (Code 10)
Device reported problems to Windows (Code 43)
Driver was blocked or is incompatible (Code 39, 52)
Hardware failure or connection issue
guides.whyItWorks: Device Manager is Windows' hardware management tool. Each device in your computer needs a driver — software that tells Windows how to communicate with it. Error codes indicate specific problems: Code 28 means no driver is installed, Code 10 means the driver loaded but the device won't start, Code 43 means the device reported a problem. By identifying the device through its Hardware ID and finding the correct driver from the manufacturer, you establish proper communication between Windows and the hardware.

steps.detail:
Open Device Manager (Windows+X > Device Manager). Look for devices with yellow warning triangles. Right-click the device > Properties > General tab. Read the 'Device status' message and note the error code.

Common codes:
• Code 10 — 'This device cannot start' — driver or hardware issue
• Code 28 — 'Drivers not installed' — need to find and install driver
• Code 31 — 'Not working properly' — reinstall driver
• Code 39 — 'Cannot load driver' — corrupted or blocked driver
• Code 43 — 'Device reported a problem' — hardware or driver failure
• Code 52 — 'Driver not signed' — needs signed driver

steps.instruction: Find the Hardware ID for unknown devices
steps.detail: For unknown devices without a name, right-click > Properties > Details tab. From the 'Property' dropdown, select 'Hardware Ids'. You'll see IDs like 'PCI\VEN_8086&DEV_1E3A' or 'USB\VID_046D&PID_C52B'. Copy the first Hardware ID. Search for this ID on Google or at devid.info to identify the device and find its driver.

Right-click the problem device > 'Update driver' > 'Search automatically for drivers'. Windows will check its driver database and Windows Update for a matching driver. If it finds one, it will install it automatically. This works for many common devices but may not find drivers for specialized hardware.

Once you know what the device is (from step 2), go to the manufacturer's website and download the driver:

• For laptops: Go to the laptop manufacturer's support page (dell.com/support, support.hp.com, support.lenovo.com), enter your model number, and download the driver
• For specific components: Go to the component manufacturer (Intel, AMD, Realtek, etc.)
• For USB peripherals: Go to the peripheral manufacturer (Logitech, etc.)

Run the downloaded installer and follow the prompts.

If updating doesn't work, do a clean reinstall. Right-click the device > 'Uninstall device'. CHECK 'Delete the driver software for this device'. Click Uninstall. Restart your computer. Then install the driver you downloaded from the manufacturer. A clean install removes any corrupted driver files that might be causing the error.

steps.instruction: Try a different USB port or check connections
steps.detail: For USB devices with Code 43 or Code 10: try a different USB port (use ports directly on the computer, not a hub). For internal hardware: power off the computer, open the case, and reseat the component (remove and re-insert it). Sometimes a loose connection causes driver errors. If the device fails in multiple ports/computers, the hardware itself may be faulty.

guides.title: Using Event Viewer to Diagnose Problems
guides.symptom: I need to figure out why my computer crashed or an application failed
guides.description: Learn to use Windows Event Viewer to find crash logs, error details, and diagnose system and application failures.
causes: Need to investigate why an application crashed
System crashed (BSOD) and need to find the cause
Service failed to start and need detailed error info
Recurring error that needs diagnosis
Security event investigation
guides.whyItWorks: Windows continuously logs every significant event — application crashes, service failures, driver errors, security events, and system state changes — to the Event Viewer. Each event has an ID, source, level (Information, Warning, Error, Critical), and detailed description. When something goes wrong, the event log contains the exact timestamp, the component that failed, and often the specific error code and description. This is the same tool professional IT technicians use to diagnose problems, and knowing how to read it transforms guesswork into informed troubleshooting.

steps.detail: Press Windows+R, type 'eventvwr.msc' and press Enter. Or search 'Event Viewer' in the Start menu. The left pane shows the log categories, the middle pane shows events, and the bottom pane shows details of the selected event.

Expand 'Windows Logs' in the left pane. The main logs are:

• Application — Application crashes, errors, and warnings (Office, browsers, games, etc.)
• System — Driver failures, service errors, Windows component issues, BSOD info
• Security — Login attempts, permission changes, audit events
• Setup — Windows Update installation logs

For most troubleshooting, start with System (for crashes and hardware) and Application (for app problems).

With a log selected, click 'Filter Current Log' in the right action pane. Check 'Critical' and 'Error' under Event Level. You can also set a time range using 'Logged' to focus on when the problem occurred. Click OK. This hides all the informational noise and shows only the problems.

Click on an error event. The bottom pane shows:

• Source — The component that logged the event (e.g., 'Application Error', 'BugCheck', 'Service Control Manager')
• Event ID — A specific number identifying the type of event. Search 'Event ID [number] [source]' on Google for explanations
• Description — Detailed text explaining what happened, often including file names, error codes, and exception details
• For BSODs: Look for Event ID 1001 from source 'BugCheck' — it contains the stop code and parameters from the blue screen

Take the Event ID number and Source from the event and search online: 'Event ID 1001 BugCheck' or 'Event ID 7034 Service Control Manager'. Microsoft's documentation and community forums often explain exactly what each event means and how to fix it. The website eventid.net is also a useful reference for common Event IDs.

steps.instruction: Create a Custom View for ongoing monitoring
steps.detail: In Event Viewer, click 'Create Custom View' in the right pane. Set Event Level to Critical and Error, select the logs you want to monitor (System and Application), and give your view a name like 'All Errors'. This appears under 'Custom Views' and gives you a single place to check all errors across multiple logs. Useful for tracking recurring problems.

steps.instruction: Export logs for sharing or analysis
steps.detail: Right-click a log > 'Save All Events As' to save as .evtx file (can be opened in Event Viewer on another PC). Or 'Save All Events As' with CSV format for analysis in Excel. This is useful when seeking help on forums or from IT support — they can analyze your event logs to diagnose the issue remotely.

guides.title: Using Reliability Monitor to Track Instability
guides.symptom: My computer has been unstable and I need to find the pattern of failures
guides.description: Use Reliability Monitor to visualize your computer's stability history, correlate crashes with changes, and identify what's causing instability.
causes: Need to identify a pattern of recurring failures
Computer became unstable after a specific change
Want to correlate software installations with crashes
Need a visual timeline of system health
guides.whyItWorks: Reliability Monitor is a user-friendly timeline that visualizes your computer's stability over time. It plots a reliability index (1-10 scale) and marks every application crash, Windows failure, hardware error, and software install/uninstall on a day-by-day timeline. By looking at this visual history, you can see exactly when problems started and what changed just before — whether it was a Windows Update, a new app installation, or a driver change. This correlation often reveals the root cause.

steps.detail: Search for 'Reliability' in the Start menu and click 'View reliability history'. Or press Windows+R, type 'perfmon /rel' and press Enter. The monitor shows a graph of your system's reliability over time with a 1-10 stability index.

The graph shows your reliability index over time. A stable system stays near 10. Drops indicate problems. Below the graph, you'll see icons for each day:

• Red X circles — Application failures and Windows failures (crashes, hangs)
• Yellow warning triangles — Miscellaneous warnings
• Blue info circles — Software install/uninstall/update events

Click on any day to see the specific events that occurred.

Look at the timeline to find when your reliability index started dropping. Click on the day just before the drop started. Check the 'Informational events' section — this shows what was installed or updated that day. If a new program was installed, a driver was updated, or a Windows Update was applied right before the instability began, that's your likely culprit.

Click on a day with failures (red X icons). The lower section shows each failure with:

• Application — Which program crashed
• Description — 'Stopped working', 'Stopped responding', etc.
• Failure bucket — Technical identifier for the specific crash type
• Date — Exact time of the failure

If the same application keeps appearing in failures, that application needs to be updated, repaired, or reinstalled.

Based on what you found:

• If a specific app keeps crashing: Update or reinstall it, check its compatibility mode settings
• If crashes started after a Windows Update: Check for newer updates that fix the issue, or uninstall the problematic update (Settings > Windows Update > Update History > Uninstall updates)
• If crashes started after a driver update: Roll back the driver (Device Manager > device > Properties > Driver tab > Roll Back)
• If crashes started after installing new software: Uninstall that software and test stability

Click 'Check for solutions to all problems' at the bottom of Reliability Monitor for automated help.

guides.title: Repair Windows When It Won't Start
guides.symptom: Windows won't boot — stuck on blue screen, black screen, or loading loop
guides.description: Complete guide to fixing Windows boot failures using recovery tools, from Automatic Repair to manual boot record reconstruction.
causes: Corrupted boot configuration data (BCD)
Bad Windows Update or driver that prevents booting
Corrupted system files essential for startup
Disk failure or file system corruption
Master Boot Record (MBR) corruption
guides.whyItWorks: Windows boot follows a specific chain: BIOS/UEFI → Boot Manager → Windows Boot Loader → Windows kernel → Desktop. If any link in this chain breaks, Windows can't start. Startup Repair automatically fixes common boot issues. bootrec commands rebuild the boot configuration database that tells the boot manager where to find Windows. SFC and DISM repair the Windows system files themselves. System Restore takes the entire system back to a known working state. Each approach targets a different part of the boot chain.

steps.detail:
If Windows won't start: Let it fail to boot 3 times in a row — Windows will automatically enter the recovery environment. You'll see 'Preparing Automatic Repair' then options appear.

Alternative methods:
• If you can reach the login screen: Hold Shift while clicking Power > Restart
• Use a Windows installation USB: Boot from USB and click 'Repair your computer'
• Force shutdown during boot by holding the power button, repeat 3 times

From Advanced Startup Options: click Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Repair. Windows will automatically diagnose and attempt to fix boot problems. This process may take 10-15 minutes. If it says it couldn't fix the problem, proceed to the next steps.

From Advanced Startup Options: Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart. Press 4 or F4 for Safe Mode. If Windows boots in Safe Mode, the problem is likely a recently installed driver or program. In Safe Mode:

• Uninstall recently installed programs
• Roll back recently updated drivers via Device Manager
• Uninstall recent Windows Updates (Settings > Update & Security > View update history > Uninstall updates)
• Run sfc /scannow in an elevated Command Prompt

Restart normally to test.

From Advanced Startup Options: Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore. Select a restore point from before the problems started. This reverts Windows system files, programs, and settings to that date WITHOUT affecting your personal files (documents, photos, etc.).
steps.warning: Programs installed after the restore point date will be removed. Your personal files are safe, but recently installed applications will need to be reinstalled.

steps.instruction: Rebuild boot records using Command Prompt
steps.detail:
From Advanced Startup Options: Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Command Prompt. Run these commands one at a time:

bootrec /fixmbr
bootrec /fixboot
bootrec /rebuildbcd

If /fixboot gives 'Access denied', run:
bcdboot C:\Windows /s C: /f ALL

These rebuild the Master Boot Record, boot sector, and Boot Configuration Data — the files that tell your computer where to find Windows.
steps.warning: These commands modify boot records. If you have multiple operating systems installed, the rebuildbcd command may affect the boot menu. Have a Windows installation USB ready as backup.

steps.detail:
From the recovery Command Prompt, run:

sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows

This scans and repairs Windows system files while Windows is offline (not running). This can fix corrupted files that prevent Windows from starting. Wait for it to complete, then type 'exit' and restart.

If nothing else works, from Advanced Startup Options: Troubleshoot > Reset this PC > Keep my files. This reinstalls Windows while preserving your personal files (documents, photos, music). You'll need to reinstall all your applications, but your data is saved.
steps.warning: IMPORTANT: 'Keep my files' preserves personal files but removes ALL installed programs and their settings. 'Remove everything' deletes ALL data — only use this if you've backed up everything important.

guides.title: Repair Disk Errors with CHKDSK
guides.symptom: I'm getting disk errors, files are corrupted, or my drive seems unhealthy
guides.description: Check and repair disk errors using CHKDSK and monitor drive health to prevent data loss.
causes: File system corruption from improper shutdown or power loss
Bad sectors developing on an aging hard drive
File system inconsistency from software crashes
Physically failing drive nearing end of life
Virus or malware damaging file system structures
guides.whyItWorks: Drives store data in organized structures — file allocation tables, directory entries, and data blocks. When these structures get damaged (from power loss, crashes, or physical drive degradation), files become inaccessible or corrupted. CHKDSK (Check Disk) scans the entire file system, verifies the integrity of every structure, fixes logical errors, and marks physically damaged sectors so the drive avoids using them. The /f flag fixes file system errors, /r locates bad sectors and recovers readable data. This is like running a health check and repair on your drive's organizational system.

steps.instruction: Check drive health with SMART data
steps.detail:
Open Command Prompt as Administrator and run:

wmic diskdrive get model,status

If status shows 'OK', the drive's self-test reports no issues. If it shows 'Pred Fail' or anything else, the drive is failing — back up immediately and replace it. For more detailed SMART data, download the free tool CrystalDiskInfo from crystalmark.info.

Open Command Prompt as Administrator and run:

chkdsk C:

This runs a read-only scan — it checks for errors but doesn't fix anything. It will report the number of errors found, if any. This is safe to run at any time and tells you if there are problems that need fixing.

To actually fix errors, run:

chkdsk C: /f /r

/f — Fixes file system errors
/r — Locates bad sectors and recovers readable information (includes /f)

For the C: drive (where Windows is installed), you'll see: 'Cannot lock drive. Would you like to schedule this to run at next restart?' Type Y and press Enter. Restart your computer — CHKDSK will run before Windows loads.
steps.warning: CHKDSK /r on a large drive can take several HOURS. Do not interrupt it or power off your computer while it's running. Run it when you won't need the computer for a while.

steps.instruction: Check Event Viewer for disk warnings
steps.detail: Open Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) > Windows Logs > System. Filter by Source = 'disk' or Source = 'ntfs'. Look for warnings or errors related to disk I/O, bad blocks, or file system issues. Recurring disk errors are a strong sign the drive is failing and needs replacement.

For solid-state drives (SSDs):

• Do NOT run chkdsk /r regularly — the extensive read/write operations can reduce SSD lifespan
• Use chkdsk /f instead (fixes file system errors without scanning for bad sectors)
• SSDs have built-in wear leveling and error correction
• Check SSD health using the manufacturer's tool (Samsung Magician, WD Dashboard, Intel SSD Toolbox, etc.)
• Enable TRIM: Open Command Prompt as Admin and run: fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify — if it returns 0, TRIM is enabled

Replace your drive immediately if:
• SMART status shows 'Pred Fail' or CrystalDiskInfo shows 'Caution' or 'Bad'
• CHKDSK keeps finding and fixing errors on every run
• You hear clicking, grinding, or unusual sounds from a hard drive
• Files randomly become corrupted or disappear
• Drive performance has dramatically decreased

Back up all important data immediately to an external drive or cloud storage before the drive fails completely.

guides.title: Fix Applications That Keep Crashing or Freezing
guides.symptom: A specific program keeps crashing, freezing, or showing 'not responding'
guides.description: Diagnose and fix application crashes and freezes through compatibility settings, clean reinstallation, and dependency repair.
causes: Corrupted application files or settings
Missing or outdated runtime dependencies (.NET, Visual C++, DirectX)
Incompatibility with current Windows version
Insufficient system resources (RAM, disk space)
Conflict with other running software or antivirus
guides.whyItWorks: Applications depend on a complex stack: the app's own files, Windows runtime libraries (.NET Framework, Visual C++ Redistributables), DirectX for graphics, sufficient system resources, and compatibility with your Windows version. When any of these are corrupted, missing, or insufficient, the app crashes. Running in compatibility mode emulates an older Windows version. Clean reinstalling (including removing leftover settings in AppData) gives the app a completely fresh start. Updating runtime dependencies ensures the foundational libraries the app needs are present and working.

steps.instruction: Check if the app meets system requirements
steps.detail: Check the application's minimum system requirements on its website. Press Windows+I > System > About to see your PC specs. Verify you have enough RAM, the right CPU, and enough disk space. Running an application below its minimum requirements will cause crashes, especially for games and professional software.

Right-click the application's shortcut or .exe file and select 'Run as administrator'. Some applications need elevated privileges to access certain files or features. If this fixes the crash, you can make it permanent: right-click > Properties > Compatibility tab > check 'Run this program as an administrator' > OK.

Right-click the application's .exe file > Properties > Compatibility tab. Check 'Run this program in compatibility mode for:' and select an older Windows version (try Windows 8 first, then Windows 7). Also try checking 'Disable fullscreen optimizations' and 'Run in 640 x 480 screen resolution' for older apps. Click Apply.

1. Uninstall the application: Settings > Apps > Apps & features > find the app > Uninstall
2. Delete leftover data: Press Windows+R, type '%appdata%' > find and delete the app's folder. Then type '%localappdata%' and do the same
3. Restart your computer
4. Download a fresh copy from the official website
5. Install the fresh copy

This removes any corrupted files or settings that were causing crashes.
steps.warning: Deleting the AppData folders removes ALL settings and saved data for that application. Export or back up any important settings from within the app first.

steps.detail:
Many apps depend on shared Windows components. Download and install the latest versions:

• Visual C++ Redistributables: Search 'Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable download' — install both x64 and x86 versions for 2015-2022
• .NET Framework: Go to Settings > Apps > Optional features > Add a feature > search '.NET Framework 3.5' and install
• .NET Runtime: Download from dotnet.microsoft.com
• DirectX: Download DirectX End-User Runtime from Microsoft

Restart after installing these components.

steps.instruction: Check Event Viewer for crash details
steps.detail:
Open Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) > Windows Logs > Application. Filter by Level = Error. Look for events with Source 'Application Error' or the app's name around the time of the crash. The details will show:

• Faulting module name — which DLL or component crashed
• Exception code — the type of crash (e.g., 0xc0000005 = access violation)

Search these details online for specific solutions. This information is invaluable when reporting bugs to the software developer.

guides.title: Fix Programs Using Too Much CPU, Memory, or Disk
guides.symptom: A program is consuming excessive CPU, memory, or disk resources
guides.description: Diagnose and control applications that consume excessive system resources, causing slowdowns and performance issues.
causes: Memory leak in the application (progressively using more RAM)
Application poorly optimized or running complex operations
Insufficient system resources for the workload
Application conflict or redundant background processes
Bug in the application causing infinite loops or excessive I/O
guides.whyItWorks: When an application uses excessive resources, it's either by design (legitimate heavy workload), by bug (memory leak, infinite loop), or by conflict (two programs fighting for the same resource). Task Manager and Resource Monitor reveal exactly what's happening — how much CPU, memory, disk, and network each process uses. Setting process priority tells Windows to give less CPU time to the resource hog. Setting CPU affinity limits which CPU cores a process can use. These are OS-level controls that work on any application without modifying it.

steps.instruction: Identify the resource usage in Task Manager
steps.detail: Press Ctrl+Shift+Esc. Click 'More details' if in simple view. On the Processes tab, click the column header for the resource that's high (CPU, Memory, or Disk) to sort. Identify which process is the top consumer. Right-click the column headers to add more columns like 'GPU' or 'Power usage'. Note the exact numbers being consumed.

steps.instruction: Use Resource Monitor for deeper analysis
steps.detail:
In Task Manager, click the Performance tab > 'Open Resource Monitor' at the bottom. Resource Monitor shows:

• CPU tab: Exact CPU time per process, service CPU usage
• Memory tab: Working set, private memory, commit, hard faults
• Disk tab: Read/write bytes per second per process, queue length
• Network tab: Network usage per process

Check the appropriate tab for your resource issue. This gives you much more detail than Task Manager.

In Task Manager, right-click the resource-heavy process > Set priority > select 'Below Normal' or 'Low'. This tells Windows to give less CPU time to this process, allowing other programs to run smoothly. The resource-heavy program will run slower but won't starve other applications.

Note: This setting resets when the program restarts. To make it permanent, you'd need a script or third-party tool.

steps.instruction: Set CPU affinity to limit CPU cores
steps.detail: In Task Manager, go to the Details tab. Right-click the process > 'Set affinity'. Uncheck some CPU cores to limit how much of your CPU the program can use. For example, on a 4-core CPU, limiting a process to 2 cores means it can only use 50% of your total CPU. This helps when an application tries to use all CPU cores.

Visit the application's website or check its settings for updates. Performance issues and memory leaks are common bugs that developers fix in updates. If you're running an older version, updating may resolve the excessive resource usage entirely.

steps.instruction: Disable hardware acceleration in the app
steps.detail: Many applications (browsers, Discord, Slack, Teams, video players) have a 'Hardware Acceleration' setting. When enabled, it offloads work to the GPU. If your GPU is weak or its driver is problematic, this can cause high CPU usage as a fallback. Find this setting in the app's settings/preferences and toggle it. In Chrome: Settings > System > 'Use hardware acceleration' > toggle off.

guides.title: Fix Software Installation and Uninstallation Failures
guides.symptom: I can't install or completely remove a program
guides.description: Resolve installation errors, stuck uninstalls, and clean up leftover software files using Windows tools and manual cleanup.
causes: Windows Installer service not running or corrupted
Previous installation left behind conflicting files
Insufficient permissions to install/uninstall
Corrupted installer file or download
Registry entries from previous installation blocking new install
guides.whyItWorks: Windows uses the Windows Installer service (MSI) to manage program installations. It tracks what files were installed, what registry entries were created, and how to undo everything during uninstallation. When this tracking database gets corrupted, or when files are left behind from a failed install, new installations can fail because the system thinks the old version is still present. Microsoft's Install/Uninstall troubleshooter fixes the tracking database. Manual cleanup of leftover files and registry entries removes the ghost of the old installation. Re-registering the Windows Installer service repairs the core installation engine.

steps.detail: Right-click the installer file (.exe or .msi) and select 'Run as administrator'. Installation often needs admin rights to write to Program Files and the Windows Registry. If running from a web browser, make sure the file is fully downloaded before running.

Press Windows+R, type 'services.msc'. Find 'Windows Installer' in the list. Make sure its status is not 'Disabled'. If it's Stopped, right-click > Start. Set Startup type to 'Manual' (this is the correct default). If you can't start it, open Command Prompt as Admin and run:

msiexec /unregister
msiexec /regserver

This re-registers the Windows Installer engine.

Download the 'Program Install and Uninstall Troubleshooter' from Microsoft's support site (search 'Microsoft program install uninstall troubleshooter'). Run the downloaded tool. Choose 'Installing' or 'Uninstalling' depending on your problem. Select the program causing issues. The tool will diagnose and fix Windows Installer database problems and leftover registry entries.

steps.instruction: Clean up leftover files from previous installation
steps.detail:
If a previous installation is blocking a new one, manually remove leftovers:

1. Delete the program's folder from C:\Program Files and C:\Program Files (x86)
2. Delete settings from %AppData% and %LocalAppData% (press Windows+R and type these paths)
3. Delete temp files: press Windows+R, type '%temp%', delete everything in the folder
4. Empty the Recycle Bin

This ensures no leftover files conflict with the new installation.
steps.warning: Make sure you're deleting the correct program's folder. Double-check the folder name before deleting.

steps.detail:
Open Registry Editor (regedit). Navigate to:

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall

and

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall

Look for a key with the program's name. If you find leftover entries for a program that's already uninstalled, right-click the key and select Delete. Also check:

HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\[program name]
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\[program name]
steps.warning: CAUTION: Deleting wrong registry entries can break other programs. Only delete entries you're certain belong to the program you're trying to clean up. Export a backup of the registry key before deleting it (right-click > Export).

steps.instruction: Run SFC and DISM for system component issues
steps.detail:
If the installation involves Windows components (like .NET Framework or Visual C++), system file corruption may be the cause. Open Command Prompt as Admin:

DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
sfc /scannow

Restart and try the installation again. This repairs the Windows component store that manages system-level installations.
